paragraphs.text: Whilst the Lord’s speaking to these seven assemblies would clearly have an historical bearing, its spiritual import is intended to affect us at the present day. His words to the angel of the assembly in Pergamos would manifestly have a current bearing on us because of the danger of the doctrine of Balaam finding entrance into what should be held unreservedly for Christ. The promises to the overcomers by the Lord Jesus would be related to the features which He discerned as already coming to light in persons who were prepared to stand for Him in those particular conditions, cost what it might. This is not drawing attention to distinctiveness of gift; it may be included, but that is not the main point. An overcomer is a man who is prepared to stand for what is right. The Lord values the moral features of quality that come to light in persons, and the Lord’s own promise to each overcomer would be related to what is already governing the heart and affections of a man or woman who is prepared to stand for Christ.
So the promise to the overcomer in Pergamos would have a rich inward bearing. What preciousness there is in this particular promise, “To him will I give of the hidden manna”.

Are we beginning to get some impressions of the glorious wealth of the hidden manna so that we are governed increasingly by it? It involves the Father’s appreciation of those hidden years of Jesus, coming out in public display as the Father’s voice was heard saying, “I have found my delight”, Luke 3: 22. Do we treasure sufficiently what the Spirit would open up to us as to the Father’s delight in Jesus during those years? How little we know of them according to the written word. We have that choice touch as to Jesus at the age of twelve. But let us make way for the Spirit as He would give us further impressions of the Father’s full delight in that hidden life. Men said that He was “the carpenter”, or “the son of the carpenter”. What delight there must have been to the Father in the Lord’s labours as the carpenter or as the son of the carpenter. Mr. Taylor referred feelingly and affectingly to how Jesus would have taken a plane, or a saw, or a chisel, (J.T. N.S. Vol. 22, p.121). No one else would have handled the carpenter’s tools as Jesus did. How the Father appreciated it! Are we appreciating it more? Are we beginning to get some impressions of the hidden manna, the secret life of Jesus with the Father? Is it governing us increasingly by way of model?

Always entering into it of course, is the intrinsic glory of His own Person as the Son with the Father. As one of the many examples of the way in which the Lord serves as a Model, think of those hidden nights on the mount of Olives—perhaps not exactly the manna, perhaps more the old corn of the land, for the mount of Olives would be a spiritual, heavenly realm, and the Lord retreated there. We have been speaking of the Lord’s departure. Let us remember that before He departed His normal resort was to the mount of Olives. It says at the end of John 7 that, “every one went to his home. But Jesus went to the mount of Olives”. I think these are the impressions that would hold a brother or sister who would desire to be an overcomer. We need to be kept near the Spirit when we think of these things. There is no place for imagination in the spiritual realm, but there is abundant scope for the blessed Spirit of truth to open up to us impressions of what the Son meant to the Father.

So the Lord says, “To him will I give of the hidden manna”. What a divine answer to the doctrine of Balaam! Another has said (and we do well to bear in mind prophetic statements of those whom the Lord has used) that the beginning and kernel of all mischief amongst us is Balaam, (J.B.S. Letters Vol. 2, p.215). Let us be on our watch. We have been reminded of watchfulness and this is something we need currently to watch in ourselves. First of all watching our own hearts and lives, then watching in our homes, and then watching in relation to the beloved brethren, the saints of God. How easy it is to make way for the doctrine of Balaam, the insidious giving way to the Moabitish element that the spirit of worldliness would bring in. O, beloved, let us cry to God that there may be a banner raised up by the Spirit, that overcomers may be raised up in every locality where the Supper is rightly being taken, so that the doctrine of Balaam may be kept at bay. May we have grace and help by the Spirit to judge the spirit of worldliness to its very roots, and to see that it has no part in a realm which is intended to be kept holy and pure for God Himself.

We do not need to go beyond our own hearts and thoughts to realise how easy it is to be governed by a spirit of worldliness. We might well in our prayers, as taking account of what God is doing universally, pray with renewed vigour that the spirit of worldliness may be judged and expelled. It will need overcomers to do it. Let us pray for overcomers. There is no need in public to name places, but in our prayers in private we might name particular localities where God is looking for men and women to stand up in the strength of the hidden manna, to stand for the rights of God and the rights of Christ in the local assembly.

Then the Lord says, “I will give to him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows but he that receives it”. The white stone, no doubt, would remind us of the purity of what is established according to God. We have been speaking together of remembrance and establishment. An overcomer is not a man to be tossed about; he is a man who himself would be taking on the features of purity according to God and of stability. One feature of an elder would be stability. He is not a man who is saying one thing one day and the opposite the next. An overcomer would be a person who in himself is taking character from Jesus as the Rock of Ages. The feature of a stone is to be worked out in us, as in Peter.

The Lord would look for each brother and sister in a locality to be an overcomer in this sense, to take on the character of persons who can be trusted to be the same. Let us take it on in holy desire to be persons who can be known as the same.

Then there is something special, “a new name written, which no one knows but he that receives it”. Are we conscious of having a personal link with the Lord Jesus? It is one of the marvels of christianity that every one of us is intended to be conscious of having a personal link with Jesus which no one else has. It needs all the saints from Pentecost to the rapture to bring out the fulness of Christ. But every one of us in variety, yet in wondrous harmony and unity, is intended to understand in a special way some impression of the glory of Jesus. Saul of Tarsus had it at the very beginning. He would never forget those words of Jesus; they provided a link between Jesus and Paul. I believe every one of us has some special impression of Christ that the Spirit would develop, and thus form us by it. Yet along with this we are to value the impressions that others have. An overcomer is not a man that stands out in his distinctiveness and rules the local assembly—he would have moral power in himself to bring out the feature of overcoming in the rest of the brethren. So the locality would merge as one man to stand for God and to be governed by the truth of what the Lord says to those at Pergamos, “He that has the sharp two-edged sword”. In John’s gospel He says, “I am … the truth”, John 14: 6.

Well, let us be governed increasingly by a desire to be here as those who would be faithful to Christ and encouraging one another to be faithful too. So may there be in every local assembly a full response according to the heart and purpose of God, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “THE FULNESS OF THE BLESSING OF CHRIST”
articles.author: J. Lovie

paragraphs.text: I think it is wonderful, dear friends, that in the glad tidings God proposes still to have man near to Him in the greatest possible blessing and in the enjoyment of His presence—not only to have man near to Him as redeemed, justified and reconciled eternally, but to have man near to Him now. In the provisional time in which we are, when sin and death are so rampant in this poor world, it is wonderful to know that God is to have men in the sense of His presence without a charge, that is, with no sense of distance, but near to Him in the blessings of the glad tidings. So that our blessings are not only for eternity, but for time. Many persons think in relation to eternity, and it is right that we should, but it is a wonderful thing to discover in your relations with God that you can come into the enjoyment of eternal blessings at the present time, to know what it is to be in the presence of God with ‘not a cloud above, not a spot within’, to know something of the unclouded sense of divine favour that shines so ineffably because of Christ who is before God in all His worth and acceptance as the One in whom we are accepted, the One who is our righteousness and our justification before Him.

So I have read these passages, following on what we had together in the reading on Romans 4, and as bearing on the thought of the righteousness of God and the blessedness of how man is accepted before God in Christ—there as justified, not only forgiven but justified. If there is anybody here who has not got the sense that their sins are forgiven, that experience is available for you tonight, right at this moment, as in faith and in repentance you put your trust in Christ. You can reach out the hand of faith as you sit on your seat. If you have never known before what it is to be forgiven, you can know right now.

God proposes freely to forgive the sinner, but to come into the enjoyment of that involves that you come in the sense of your need as a repenting sinner, stretching out the hand of faith and taking God at His word, laying claim to the blessing that God offers through faith in believing. What an Object for faith Jesus is! How wondrous the work of atonement He has done when He suffered in the sinner’s stead and bore the judgment of God due to sin. He was the Victim in the darkness of Calvary’s woe. He took the sinner’s place, bore the judgment due to the sinner, and He exhausted that judgment. He said, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”, Psalm 22: 1. Why was it that God hid His face from Christ as the Sin bearer in the darkness of the cross? It was because God is holy (Psalm 22: 3) and in order that you and I, through faith in believing, night come into the sense of God’s unclouded favour and know the experience of forgiveness, in virtue of the work and the shed blood of Jesus.

Then we are to know not only that we are forgiven but that we are justified. I know I am justified in the fact that the One who died for me on the cross now lives in heaven in the presence of God. He is there as my righteousness and my peace before God. Oh the unclouded joy of coming into God’s favour in the worth of the Man who fills His presence, knowing that He is there as your righteousness, that God regards you as you approach Him as righteous, because the Saviour who died for you on the cross is now in His presence exalted. There is no trace of sin—it is all gone—

‘My sins—not in part, but the whole—
Were borne on the cross, and are gone evermore’.

They will never come up again; God will never raise again the matter of your sins because Jesus has borne those sins in His body on the tree, and as through faith and believing you lay claim to the precious Saviour tonight God regards you as justified, because Jesus, the One who has borne your sins, is now alive in His presence, a glorified Saviour.

These Galatian brethren were tending to go back to law, to think that they could be justified on the principle of law, and Paul brings in the elements of the gospel to meet this error. He points out that Christ has redeemed us out of the curse of the law. This is a very affecting matter that in the Galatian epistle redemption is from the curse of the law. Paul says, “having become a curse for us, (for it is written, Cursed is every one hanged upon a tree)”. The Lord Jesus took on the whole matter of the curse, took it on vicariously; it did not belong to Him, precious Saviour that He is. He took it on vicariously for you and for me. He took up the whole matter of the curse, and bore it Himself as hanging upon the tree. He took on the shame and the ignominy and the scandal of the cross, the Lord took on these things vicariously so that you and I should not know the curse, but that we should know the ineffable blessedness of divine favour and joy.

So it says, “that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith”. So it is that God proposes in the glad tidings the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit, the blessing of Abraham coming to the nations. God is coming out to men everywhere on the basis of the new covenant in His unconditional proposals to bless. He is coming out in the blessing of Abraham, reaching out to the nations, that we should receive the promise of the Spirit. These two great thoughts are linked together in the glad tidings, that is, the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit. It is then, dear brethren, that this is all presented to us from the divine side.

I have read from Luke’s gospel as he brings forward a daughter of Abraham and a son of Abraham. Luke, who writes in the gain of Paul’s ministry, and the blessing of Abraham coming out to the nations, shows how Joseph’s branches have reached over the wall. They have reached to you and to me, who are of the nations. In Luke 13 we have the daughter of Abraham and it says, “whom Satan has bound, lo, these eighteen years”. Think of the length of time that this poor woman with a spirit of infirmity had been bent together and wholly unable to lift her head up! That is the situation in chapter 13 of Luke. The Lord in His ministry of grace is drawing near and He is healing her on the sabbath day. God is doing that.

It is really how grace is out in all its beneficence to meet every need in Luke, the Lord being available in relation to every needy soul. This woman had been bowed down for eighteen years. Think of the length of that time! She has not been available to look up, or to stand up straight; nor had she been available in the praise of God. The Lord draws near in the ministry of grace, no matter how long the time this condition has obtained. He draws near and heals her on the sabbath day. It is then that the Lord identifies Himself in grace with this condition with a view to its alleviation and removal.

A wondrous thing this; no matter how long we may have continued in a certain way—this woman went on for eighteen years—the Lord in grace identifies Himself with the condition. He says, “Thou art loosed from thine infirmity”. He laid His hands upon her and immediately she was made straight and glorified God. Think of the divine ideal in securing this woman.

God made man upright; He made him straight. It says that immediately she was made straight, and glorified God. Then the Lord said, “Ought she not to be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?”—this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound these eighteen years. What a thing it is then to be loosed. The Lord loosed her from what was holding her. The Lord could do that tonight. He could loose every soul from whatever hindrance is holding them.

You remember what Samson said to the young man who held him, he said, “Let loose of me”, Judges 16: 26. That is, through exercise he got free from some influence that was holding him. That is how it would affect you and me, that we concern ourselves to say, “Let loose of me”. That would be our side, that whatever hindrance, whatever it may be that is hindering, whatever element of prejudice, or resistance, may be in our hearts, in relation to the great thoughts of God, we shake ourselves free from it.

Here the Lord loosed this woman. He did it. O, we could never have loosed ourselves from that bondage and burden of restraint. The Lord did it in His grace. He said, “Thou art loosed from thine infirmity”. O, dear brethren, what a day this is in the soul of any person, however long they may have gone on in this condition of bondage, maybe bowed down for eighteen years. It says He laid His hands upon her. That is what grace did to this woman, a daughter of Abraham. She is extending the line of the family of faith. Abraham is the father of the faith family, and God set out in that dear man, through this progenitive way, the great thought of the family of faith.

Then when we come to chapter 19, we get a son of Abraham, Zacchaeus. He is little of stature; he wants to see Jesus and climbs up into a sycamore tree, for He is passing that way. As the Lord came to the place He looked up and saw him. The Lord knew Zacchaeus was there. He looked up and saw him, and said, “Zacchaeus, make haste and come down, for today I must remain in thy house”. What a touch of grace this is! What a touch this is of the blessing of Abraham, involving the obedience of faith, and involving how the house is to be affected by the great thought of baptism.

I think Zacchaeus would come into the light of that; he “obeyed from the heart the form of teaching into which ye were instructed”, that is, he would obey the teaching of baptism, the teaching of Romans 6. The Lord says, “today I must remain in thy house”. There were those who complained that the Lord had turned in to lodge with a sinful man. Then Zacchaeus shows how much he is in the gain of—not only adding the fifth part, that was a requisite under the law that you pay the fifth part—but he says, “I return him fourfold”. He was prepared to recompense four hundred per cent. That is what grace can do in a son of Abraham as he gets this word from Christ. And Jesus says, “Today salvation is come to this house, inasmuch as he also is a son of Abraham; for, the Son of man has come to seek and to save that which is lost”. So it is, dear brethren, that Paul says, “that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith”.

Now, when Paul proposes to come to Rome he says, “But I know that, coming to you, I shall come in the fulness of the blessing of Christ”. O, I think this is the light of Ephesians, “the fulness of the blessing of Christ”. It is more than your relief, and mine, from the bondage of sin. It is how God proposes to have men for Himself, for His own pleasure and joy. God has nothing less in His heart for you and for me than that we should come into the wondrous enjoyment of His favour, to be before Him without a cloud, before Him as accepted in the Beloved, knowing that the place that Christ enjoys in the Father’s favour, is the place that God has in His mind for men, “the fulness of the blessing of Christ”.

How blessed to be there as suited for the presence of the God who sought our blessing, and to know that, through divine grace and divine working, we are not only forgiven, we are not only justified and have the gift of God’s Spirit, but we are brought to be at home in the presence of God with the sense that we are taken into favour in the Beloved. I think this is “the fulness of the blessing of Christ”. Paul proposes to come to the nations with this. He says, “I will set off by you into Spain. But I know that, coming to you I shall come in the fulness of the blessing of Christ”. He has nothing less in his affections for the brethren than that they should come into the enjoyment of the unbounded, illimitable favour of God; to know that favour shining in a Man in His presence, who is there as our righteousness and our justification.

May the Lord grant, dear brethren, that the precious fruits of the glad tidings may be more effective in us, to know what it is to be at home in the presence of the God who has sought our blessing, who has made it possible through the work that Jesus has done that we should be before Him with the sense of His favour, as taken into favour in the Beloved. It is what God in His favour extends to the nations in the One who is in His presence as Man. That can be your experience and mine as we come by way of repentance through faith in believing and in the experience of the gift of the Spirit and the enjoyment of the favour of God.

articles.title: “SO ALSO IS THE CHRIST”
articles.author: J. A. Petersen
articles.place: Word at a meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: I felt it right to add a word to what has already been said by our brother as to the name of Jesus. It is right to ‘add’, as David said to Solomon, “and thou shalt add to it”, 1 Chronicles 22: 14. Solomon in that way would give a certain fulness to what David had given to the house. Again, in the Acts, “the Lord added to the assembly daily those that were to be saved”, Acts 2: 47. This would refer to the personnel and it would be the exercise here and in other localities that the Lord might add—add persons to be with us in the truth. We should look for this. In early Acts it was not a question of anything being added to the assembly in an essential way, for all was there in that the Holy Spirit had come. In this sense nothing was added; but what is referred to is persons being added.

What is in mind in the passages read is to add something to what our brother has said as to the name of Jesus. In John 9 the blind man speaks of “a man called Jesus”, showing that he was coming into accord with heaven as to that Man. Genesis 5 would help us to see something further involving mystery, that is, the Spirit speaks of Adam and Eve as “them” and God “called their name Adam”. That is, the woman is included in the name given to Adam. “Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created”. What is current in christendom generally is something of the Man (and we thank God for all that is rightly said of Him), but little or nothing is understood of the assembly. What is next Christ’s heart is the assembly, and as we are near Him we shall soon discover what His interests are, as Exodus shows—“I love my master, my wife, and my children”, Exodus 21: 5. If we go into a brother’s home we find what is next to his heart, that is, his wife, and his children. So, as to Christ and the assembly, the hymn says, ‘Upon His throne, in glory bright, the bride of Christ shall be’. In the recent three-day meetings here we were helped by our brother Mr. Hammond to see that the assembly has, and ever will have, the nearest place of all the families to divine Persons.
We should ponder the meaning of the Spirit of God in the way He speaks in Genesis 5, including the woman with the man in the name given, “and called their name Adam”.

Brethren will recall that the prophet Isaiah speaks of seven women who say to one man, “only let us be called by thy name” (Isaiah 4: 1). They say, “Take away our reproach”, meaning, I take it, that the believer is in reproach before his enemies and before God unless he has the name of that Man on him. “And, by faith in his name, his name has made this man strong” (Acts 3: 16): thus Peter silenced the enemies as to what had transpired with the lame man. He adds later, “And salvation is in none other, for neither is there another name under heaven which is given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4: 12). What protection, what salvation and what deliverance!—“The name of the God of Jacob protect thee”, Psalm 20: 1. The reference in Genesis 5, however, involves mystery and the secret side as to the name, and we have to understand it through Paul’s ministry as to Christ and the assembly.

The passage in 1 Corinthians 12 involves the mysterious side in our links with Christ as in the body, involving the operations of the Holy Spirit. We have been helped in ministry to understand this expression, “so also is the Christ”. It is the anointed position, involving ourselves as included in the body. As we have been taught, it is His body—that is, Christ over again as seen in the saints. Think of being included in this thought, “so also is the Christ”. It is not just Christ by Himself but also Christ as in, and seen in, His saints in the body. “But all the members of the body, being many, are one body, so also is the Christ”. I think we should ponder how the thought of the name, in this way, extends to the saints. Thus we see, as in the Acts, that publicly that name gives us protection, salvation, power, and deliverance, and then in this mysterious and secret way we also have our link with Christ, “so also is the Christ”.
May the Lord bless the word.

One was impressed on Lord’s day with the thought of the good Shepherd and the reality and glory of a manhood that was wholly delightful to the Father. I thought about David—what a man he was! We have often been reminded of the way that he was sovereignly chosen to lead the people of God. Israel, as a nation, as it says, “He chose David his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds—From following the suckling-ewes, he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance”. What a shepherd David was! From early years, as a lad, he was tending the flock of his father. What a service that is, beloved; one feels very tested in speaking about it. How little we measure up to these men, and yet the Lord has laid hold of each one of us so that some feature might come out in us that would reflect divine feelings for what is in our localities.

It says, “He brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance”. How often we are reminded of what God has so peculiarly for His own pleasure. He had it, no doubt, in David’s day; David was raised up to this and, that the people might be secured for God’s praise and glory. David reached it at the end of his days, though the filling out of the service was left to Solomon, his son. In the meantime, “He fed them according to the integrity of his heart, and led them by the skilfulness of his hands”. O, beloved, what features belong to men of shepherd character, and how many there are in the Scriptures. There is only time to refer to David and what was reached in him, despite the breakdown and failure that belonged to his day and even to himself. I believe it is a link with our own day, when the enemy has wrought so extensively. But, thank God, there are men that we can call shepherds, and it is open to every one of us, in our measure, to strive to this end, to feed the sheep and to lead them.

Then we can speak about Jesus Himself. In John, as we know, the glory of His Person shines; who He was as the Son of God and taking on this beautiful character of a Shepherd, as He says, “I am the good shepherd”. No one could compare with Jesus. There is no one like Him, beloved, serving the sheep and bringing them into the greatest thoughts that God has in mind for them. It is a very tender, affectionate term, ‘shepherd’, and the character of it comes out in the gospels. “I am the good shepherd; and I know those that are mine, and am known of those that are mine, as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep”. Who else could lay down his life for the sheep? We have been reminded of David, and I suppose he went at the risk of his life when he slew the lion and the bear; but Jesus laid down His life for the sheep. O, what a shepherd character belongs to Jesus and to Him alone!
That would affect us. It affected us as we were at the Supper on Lord’s day, the character of Man in whom the Father found infinite delight, who lay down His life for the sheep.
Then He has other sheep “which are not of this fold—those also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one flock, one shepherd”. O, we look forward to that day!

Today is a broken day—how few the sheep are who are prepared to walk in the light of the truth; but the Supper reminds us of the many—not that we are able to walk with all—and we hold them in the light of the one flock, one Shepherd. “On this account the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it again. No one takes it from me”. O, the wonder of these statements! “I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down and I have authority to take it again”. How wonderful it is that a divine Person Himself has come into manhood and laid down His life—“I have received this commandment of my Father”. It does our affections good to be occupied with this blessed Man, the true Shepherd, who lay down His life for the sheep, having in mind, as seen typically in David, the inheritance, what was to come in that would yield infinite pleasure to His own heart and to the heart of the Father.

Paul, in Acts 20, is seen as taking character from his Master. He says to the Ephesian elders, “Take heed therefore to yourselves, and to all the flock”. What difficult days they were! Paul adds, as to the flock, “wherein the Holy Spirit has set you as overseers”—we would desire to be amongst the overseers, would we not, in the locality? The Lord has, I believe, deep delight in the local assembly and He has set men there as overseers. They are to shepherd the assembly of God. We should think about them universally, these shepherds, men prepared to lay down their lives in relation to the assembly of God, which is precious to the heart of Christ and to the Father.

Paul goes on to refer to “the assembly of God, which he has purchased with the blood of his own”. O, the value, the purchase price, of the assembly! What a tender, affectionate term that is—“the blood of his own”. We think of the perfection of Christ’s manhood, the life that was laid down—“the blood of his own”. How the Father felt it; how the Lord Jesus felt it; but if the flock was to be secured—“one flock, one shepherd”—it meant that the good Shepherd must lay down His life for the sheep. Well, what are the results, beloved; what are they in this place?
As we think of what the Lord has secured in His own, may there be much more from us, for His own heart’s satisfaction and to the glory of the Father, for His name’s sake.

It seems to me, dear brethren, a matter of encouragement and profit to consider that God always has us each in mind. He does not forget us, even in our ordinary affairs, our ordinary circumstances; He is thinking about us, what we do and what we say and where we go. God is never forgetting us in the way of sympathy, as this scripture in the psalm brings out. There is nothing quite like the interest of a father in his son or in his children. Some feature of progress, some further feature of intelligence, comes to light in a child; the father is interested in that, takes account of it, nothing is missed. In the same way God takes account of us with sympathetic interest. This passage refers to those that fear Him. We live in a day, dear brethren, when many do not fear God, but we are to be amongst those who fear Him. There is encouragement in this scripture to see the gain of being thought of sympathetically by God as Father as we are amongst those who fear Him, involving how we go about our ordinary affairs.

I am impressed with the need to maintain faithfulness in its detail when we are away from one another. Circumstances are difficult, yet God as Father is entering into them, taking account of what they involve in their detail and remembering what we are, even physically.

How affecting that is, that God is able to enter even into that!—“Himself knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust”. Now it is more important to pay attention, beloved, to how God thinks about things than to the reaction men might have to our behaviour, because, after all, as it says here, man is passing. What matters is how God sees things and what His attitude is to them; not any standard that may be arrived at by common consent as to anything, because what is arrived at on that line will be a lowering of things. But the divine standard will be maintained by us, I believe, as we are occupied with Christ and with what is due to God as it has been set forth in Christ. Let us, therefore, see the matter of how man will view things in its proper light, for this scripture shows that man as such (the word involving weakness, ‘mortal man’) is passing. But on the other hand God is taking account in sympathetic interest of those who fear Him, and His loving-kindness is upon them. It is something to consider, beloved, that faithfulness in one generation is often honoured by continuance coming to light in another generation. So it says, “the loving-kindness of Jehovah is from everlasting and to everlasting, upon them that fear him, and his righteousness unto children’s children, To such as keep his covenant and to those that remember his precepts to do them”.
So that if God is not forgetting about us, beloved, do not let us forget about His precepts, do not let us by-pass them when we are in a strait or in a difficulty, let us remember them.

The law was to be made prominent and kept near to the people in the old dispensation; it was to be read frequently and it was to be bound upon them, showing that we are to be concerned for what is for God as priests, to know the divine standard of things and to be concerned as to its maintenance, so that this enjoyment of conscious favour from God should be our portion as we think of His sympathetic interest in us as amongst those that fear Him. Then, too, we should think of the Lord Jesus as bearing the saints on His heart continually.

This section in Exodus has in view particularly our going in to God, and surely our concern is increasingly to have greater substantial part in the service of God in its reality, so every one is held by Christ in connection with the matter of going in. That seems to be stressed in connection with Aaron here, that it is “when he goes into the sanctuary, for a memorial before Jehovah continually”. And what comes in in connection with this is this matter of the Urim and the Thummim which was referred to when we read the scripture here recently. I was impressed with it at the time that the divine standard is set out there. So the Lord Jesus is not lowering things at all, but He has us in mind according to the standard which He Himself has set forth as here, that we should be maintained according to that standard in view of going in to God. And, beloved, as we all know, our experience of going in to God is affected practically by how we are day by day in our ordinary affairs. But the Lord Jesus has us all upon His heart. How touching it is to think of that in its wider bearing in these days when so many have turned aside and when distance has come in. Beloved, the Lord Jesus has every one in mind and in His affection He is carrying each one. We are to be stimulated by this to see to our own state in view of more substantial entrance into the service of God.

I thought that in John 17 we have an illustration of how the true Aaron is bearing us on His heart in going in to God. It has its bearing on the whole dispensation and, beloved, the standard is that the saints are not of the world as Christ was not of the world. There is no other standard for us than that, and if it is not maintained we shall not have full entrance into, and enjoyment of, the service of God at its true level. Then the Lord’s service is continually available to us, “Sanctify them by the truth—thy word is truth”. How continuously the Lord serves us in sanctification in meetings such as these, and others. His thoughts are directed to what is to be for God and maintained in fulness in the service of God, even if the days are difficult. The Lord Jesus is maintaining things according to God at their true level. He would, I believe, provoke our sympathetic interest, so that we should participate in the maintenance of what is due to God here as priests, upholding divine principles and maintaining the standard of our walk in view of increase in the service of God, for His name’s sake.
